extracted.intended_audience: essayists and literary critics; educated general readers interested in moral/periodical essays
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing short moral and critical essays in the Spectator tradition: how to select subjects, handle criticism, avoid offense, and portray characters/themes (aging, love, solitude, marriage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude news and partisan politics
rubrics_metrics.description: My paper has not in it a single Word of News, a Reflection in Politics, nor a Stroak of Party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid including news items, political reflections, or party polemics in this kind of moral/periodical essay; the author argues that removing party and news keeps discourse temperate and draws readers toward virtue and morality rather than factional heat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid loose, immoral, obscene or scandalous material
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no Fashionable Touches of Infidelity, no obscene Ideas, no Satyrs upon Priesthood, Marriage, and the like popular Topics of Ridicule; no private Scandal, nor any Thing that may tend to the Defamation of particular Persons, Families, or Societies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from using sensational, obscene, irreligious, or scandal-driven content even if it would sell; the paper should not trade on defamation or coarse ridicule and should promote moral improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect private reputations when criticizing
rubrics_metrics.description: I am at pains in qualifying what I write after such a manner, that nothing may be interpreted as aimed at private Persons. When I draw any faulty Character, I consider all those Persons to whom the Malice of the World may possibly apply it, and take care to dash it with such particular Circumstances as may prevent all such ill-natured Applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing criticism or satirical character sketches, shape descriptions so they cannot easily be mapped onto real individuals; include distinguishing particulars that prevent malicious identification and be sensitive to readers' reputations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose fictional names carefully to avoid resemblance
rubrics_metrics.description: When I place an imaginary Name at the Head of a Character, I examine every Syllable and Letter of it, that it may not bear any Resemblance to one that is real.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check invented names at the syllable/letter level to ensure they don't closely resemble real persons' names—this is a concrete precaution to avoid unintended libel or personal offence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid giving offence to public/high figures
rubrics_metrics.description: I have taken more than ordinary Care not to give Offence to those who appear in the higher Figures of Life. I would not make myself merry even with a Piece of Paste-board that is invested with a Publick Character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steer clear of ridicule directed at prominent public figures or public ceremonies; though such topics may offer easy amusement, refrain from exploiting them in order to preserve civility and avoid unnecessary offence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim of criticism: discover beauties and excellences, not merely expose faults
rubrics_metrics.description: The Criticisms which I have hitherto published, have been made with an Intention rather to discover Beauties and Excellencies in the Writers of my own Time, than to publish any of their Faults and Imperfections. In the mean while I shall ... endeavour to do Justice to those who have distinguished themselves ... and to point out such Beauties in their Works as may have escaped the Observation of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize identifying and explaining positive merits in works under review; use criticism to illuminate and improve appreciation rather than to tear down—this governs tone, selection of examples, and purpose of reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present criticism as private opinion and invite better remarks
rubrics_metrics.description: I shall not however presume to impose upon others my own particular Judgment on this Author, but only deliver it as my private Opinion. 'Si quid novisti rectius istis, Candidus imperti; si non, his utere mecum.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame critical judgments as personal and provisional; invite readers and fellow critics to contribute superior observations candidly rather than treating one's view as authoritative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lecture on growing old: counsel against attachment to transients and show change
rubrics_metrics.description: In such a Lecture you must propose, that no one set his Heart upon what is transient; the Beauty grows wrinkled while we are yet gazing at her. The witty Man sinks into a Humourist imperceptibly, for want of reflecting that all Things around him are in a Flux, and continually changing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing about ageing, emphasize human change and impermanence, warn readers against valuing only transient pleasures, and illustrate by showing how tastes, company, and advantages shift over years; use examples that render consequences tangible (e.g., wit becoming affectation, envy of younger people).

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict courtship and marriage with moral realism: long courtship and character over show
rubrics_metrics.description: The pleasantest Part of a Man's Life is generally that which passes in Courtship ... Those Marriages generally abound most with Love and Constancy, that are preceded by a long Courtship. A good Person does not only raise, but continue Love ... Good-Nature and Evenness of Temper will give you an easie Companion for Life; Virtue and good Sense, an agreeable Friend; Love and Constancy, a good Wife or Husband.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray romantic relationships valuing sustained courtship and intrinsic qualities (virtue, good sense, good-nature, constancy) over mere beauty, fashion, or fortune. Advise writers to show pre-marriage scrutiny (be inquisitive about faults) and post-marriage forbearance (discretion and good-nature to soften imperfections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray solitude and eccentricity sincerely, not as mere affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: It has been from Age to Age an Affectation to love the Pleasure of Solitude ... The best way of separating a Man's self from the World, is to give up the Desire of being known to it ... many who affect their own Way do it out of a Sourness and Spirit of Contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing characters who live apart or affect eccentricity, distinguish genuine motives (contented withdrawal, private charity, principled simplicity) from pose or contrarianism. Use concrete portraits (e.g., the charitable 'humourist' vs. the affected 'Irus') to show the moral and social consequences of sincere versus insincere solitude.
